entry: Apparent shape of the Moon's sunlit portion as viewed from Earth. Because the Moon is [[Tidal locking|tidally locked]] to Earth, the cycle of phases takes one lunar month, which averages about 29.5 days. The four major phases are the new moon, first quarter, [[Full moon|full moon]], and last quarter. The four minor phases are waxing crescent, waxing gibbous, waning gibbous, and waning crescent. The sunlit portion ranges from 0% at new moon to nearly 100% at full moon. Appearance varies with latitude and differs between the Northern and Southern hemispheres.

Meal typically eaten around the middle of the day, between [[Breakfast|breakfast]] and [[Dinner|dinner]]. Its form, size, and significance vary across cultures and historical periods; in some societies lunch is the main meal of the day, while elsewhere it is lighter and more utilitarian. Foods range from [[Sandwich|sandwiches]] and [[Salad|salads]] to more elaborate meals with rice, noodles, or [[Soup|soups]]. The Oxford English Dictionary calls the word's origin uncertain; it was first recorded in 1591 with the meaning "thick piece, hunk." In England during the late 17th and 18th centuries, dinner moved into the evening and lunch filled the gap. Until the early 19th century, luncheon was generally reserved for women and was a light meal, often of leftovers from the previous night's dinner.

Malignant tumor that originates in the tissues of the [[Lung|lungs]]. Most cases are caused by [[Tobacco smoking|tobacco smoking]], while the rest stem from exposure to hazardous substances such as [[Asbestos|asbestos]] and [[Radon|radon]] gas, or from genetic mutations that arise by chance. Without treatment, tumors spread through the lung and eventually [[Metastasis|metastasize]]. Early disease often has no symptoms; later symptoms are typically nonspecific respiratory problems, such as coughing, shortness of breath, or chest pain. Around 85% of cases are non-small-cell cancers, including adenocarcinomas and squamous-cell carcinomas, and 15% are small-cell. Early-stage tumors are treated with [[Surgery|surgery]], sometimes followed by [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]] and [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]]. Even with treatment, around 20% of people survive five years after diagnosis. Lung cancer is the most diagnosed and deadliest cancer worldwide, with 2.2 million cases and 1.8 million deaths in 2020.

Class of freshwater [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] in the [[Sarcopterygii|lobe-finned fish]] group, also called dipnoans. Lungfish breathe air with lungs homologous to those of tetrapods, and they are the closest living relatives of the [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]], which include amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Only six species survive, in [[Africa]], [[South America]], and [[Australia]], although the group was once distributed worldwide. Their fossil record extends into the Early [[Devonian]], more than 410 million years ago. Lungfish have crushing tooth plates for hard-shelled prey and the largest genome among vertebrates.

Prefecture-level city in western [[Henan]] province, China (pop., 2022: 7.079 million). Its name refers to its location on the north, or sunny ("yang"), side of the Luo River, and it lies at the confluence of the Luo and [[Yellow River|Yellow]] rivers. Among the oldest cities in China, Luoyang is the earliest of the Four Great Ancient Capitals. The Duke of Zhou built the settlement of Chengzhou in 1036 BC, and Wangcheng became the capital of the [[Zhou dynasty|Eastern Zhou dynasty]] in 771 BC. In AD 25, Emperor Guangwu made the city the capital of the Eastern [[Han dynasty]]. Under [[Wu Zetian]], the only female emperor in Chinese history, it was called Shendu, or "divine capital." It regained the name Luoyang in 1912.

Mexico-born actress and author. Nyong'o was raised mainly in [[Nairobi]], Kenya, and made her professional debut at 14 as Juliet in [[William Shakespeare|William Shakespeare's]] *Romeo and Juliet*. She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for *12 Years a Slave* (2013). Her later films include *Black Panther* (2018), *Us* (2019), and *The Wild Robot* (2024). She was nominated for a Tony Award for her role in the play *Eclipsed* (2015). Her children's book *Sulwe* (2019) became a number-one *New York Times* best-seller, and she has twice been nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award for narrating the documentary series *Serengeti*.

[[Autoimmune disease|Autoimmune]] disease, formally called systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), affecting many parts of the body. Symptoms include painful, swollen joints, fever, chest pain, hair loss, mouth ulcers, and a red rash, most often on the face. The name is Latin for "wolf," given in the 13th century because the rash was thought to resemble a wolf's bite. The cause is unclear but involves genetics and environmental factors, including sunlight, smoking, [[Vitamin D|vitamin D]] deficiency, and certain infections. SLE greatly raises the risk of [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]], the most common cause of death. Women of childbearing age are affected about nine times more often than men. There is no cure.

Capital and largest city of [[Zambia]] (pop., 2022: 2,204,059), on the central plateau at an elevation of about 1,279 m (4,196 ft). One of the fastest-developing cities in [[Southern Africa]], it is the center of Zambia's commerce and government and is connected to the country's four main highways. English is the official language of city administration, while Bemba, Tonga, and Chichewa are common street languages. Settlement dates to at least the 6th century, and the modern city was founded in 1905 as a water stop on a railway built by the British South African Company to link Copperbelt mines to [[Cape Town]]. Named after a local Lenje chief, it was chosen in 1929 as the capital of the British colonial administration of Northern Rhodesia, replacing Livingstone. It became capital of independent Zambia in 1964, followed by a building program that included the University of Zambia and a new airport.

Intense desire for something, such as sexual activity, [[Money|money]], or [[Power (political science)|power]], as well as food, as distinct from the need for it. Lust is distinguished from passion, which in properly ordered form pursues benevolent goals. [[Religion|Religions]] tend to treat lust as immoral when its object is improperly ordered, while passion is considered God-given and moral. In [[Judaism]], the *yetzer hara*, or evil inclination, is not a demonic force but the misuse of things the body needs, and the [[Torah]] is considered its great antidote. [[Thomism]], which draws on [[Aristotle]], distinguishes the intellect, will, and appetite. In many translations of the [[New Testament]], "lust" renders a Greek word that was a general term for desire, although in English the word is often associated with sex.

Plucked [[String instrument|string instrument]] with a neck and a deep, round back enclosing a hollow cavity, either fretted or unfretted. More specifically, the term usually refers to the European family, which shares a common ancestor with the modern Near-Eastern oud. The name may derive from [[Arabic|Arabic]] *al-ʿoud*, "the wood." One hand plucks the strings while the other presses them against the fingerboard to change pitch. In the [[Renaissance]] the lute was the most important instrument for secular music, and in the [[Baroque music|Baroque]] era it played the basso continuo, improvising [[Chord (music)|chords]] from a figured bass or following written parts. Being small, it produces a relatively quiet sound. A lute player is a lutenist, and a maker of lutes is a luthier.

Silvery white metal, the [[Chemical element|chemical element]] with symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It is the last element of the [[Lanthanide|lanthanide]] series and is traditionally counted among the rare earth elements. It resists corrosion in dry air but not in moist air. It was independently discovered in 1907 by Georges Urbain, Carl Auer von Welsbach, and Charles James, all of whom found it as an impurity in [[Ytterbium|ytterbium]]. Urbain was granted naming priority and called the element lutecium, after Lutetia, the Latin name for [[Paris|Paris]]; the spelling was changed to lutetium in 1949. It is significantly more common than [[Silver|silver]] in Earth's crust. Lutetium-176, a radioisotope with a [[Half-life|half-life]] of about 38 billion years, is used to date minerals and [[Meteorite|meteorites]]. Lutetium-177 is used in radionuclide therapy for neuroendocrine tumors.

American R&B and soul singer, songwriter, and record producer. He achieved eleven consecutive RIAA-certified platinum albums and sold over 40 million records worldwide. Vandross began as a backing vocalist for artists including [[Bette Midler|Bette Midler]], [[Diana Ross|Diana Ross]], and [[David Bowie|David Bowie]], and in 1981 he released his debut solo album, *Never Too Much*. He won eight [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]], including Song of the Year in 2004 for "Dance with My Father." His duets include "The Closer I Get to You" with [[Beyoncé|Beyoncé]] and "Endless Love" with [[Mariah Carey|Mariah Carey]]. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame|Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

Major branch of [[Protestantism|Protestantism]] arising from the work of [[Martin Luther|Martin Luther]], a 16th-century German friar whose efforts to reform the [[Catholic Church|Catholic Church]] helped launch the [[Reformation|Reformation]] in 1517. Lutheran churches adhere to the Bible and the ecumenical creeds, and their doctrine is set out in the Book of Concord. Lutherans teach justification by grace alone, through faith alone, on the basis of Scripture alone, with tradition subordinate to Scripture, whereas the Roman Catholic Church holds that final authority comes from both Scripture and tradition. Though not dogmatic about the number of sacraments, Lutherans generally recognize baptism, confession, and the [[Eucharist|Eucharist]]. Lutheranism became the [[State religion|state church]] of many parts of Northern Europe, beginning with Prussia in 1525, and it numbers 90 million worldwide.

Landlocked [[Western Europe|Western European]] country, officially the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, bordered by [[Belgium|Belgium]], Germany, and France. Its capital, Luxembourg City, is one of the four institutional seats of the European Union and hosts the Court of Justice of the European Union. It is a representative democracy headed by a constitutional monarch, making it the world's only remaining sovereign grand duchy. The County of Luxembourg was established in the 11th century as a state within the [[Holy Roman Empire|Holy Roman Empire]]; the country was later annexed by France and partitioned three times, and it regained independence in 1867 after the Luxembourg Crisis. Luxembourgish is the national language, while French is the sole language for legislation. A [[Developed country|developed country]] with one of the world's highest PPP-adjusted GDPs per capita, it is a founding member of the European Union, the [[OECD|OECD]], the United Nations, [[NATO|NATO]], and the Benelux. Its historic city was declared a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1994.

City in Upper [[Egypt|Egypt]] on the [[Nile|Nile]] (pop., 2023: 284,952), formerly known as Thebes. Among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, it was the capital of Upper Egypt during the New Kingdom and the city of the god [[Amun|Amun]]. The ruins of the [[Temple|temple]] complexes at Karnak and Luxor stand within the modern city, and it has often been characterized as "the world's greatest open-air museum." Across the Nile lies the West Bank Theban Necropolis, including the [[Valley of the Kings|Valley of the Kings]], burial ground of pharaohs such as [[Tutankhamun|Tutankhamun]]. Around 5 million tourists arrive annually, and the city is known for its hot air balloons.

Largest and most populous island in the [[Philippines|Philippines]] (pop., 2024: 64.3 million), in the northern part of the archipelago. It is the country's economic and political center, and its capital, [[Manila|Manila]], and [[Quezon City|Quezon City]], the most populous city, both lie on the island. Luzon is the 4th most populous island in the world and the 15th largest by land area. Its name may derive from *lusong*, a Tagalog word for a large wooden mortar used to dehusk rice. The oldest known Philippine document, the Laguna Copperplate Inscription, dates to AD 900 and names places around Manila Bay. Before AD 1000, Tagalog, Kapampangan, and Pangasinan peoples had established coastal polities such as Maynila, Tondo, and Namayan. Fossils of the extinct archaic human *Homo luzonensis*, found in Callao Cave, date to at least 50,000 to 67,000 years ago.

Sixth-largest city in [[Ukraine|Ukraine]] (pop., 2025: 723,403) and administrative center of Lviv Oblast. Named after Leo I of Galicia, it was the capital of the [[Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia|Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia]] from 1272 to 1340, when King [[Casimir III the Great|Casimir III the Great]] of Poland took it. It was granted town rights in 1356, and in 1772 it became capital of the Habsburg Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria. Its culture, industry, and academic institutions flourished between 1918 and 1939 in the Second Polish Republic. After the [[Soviet Union|Soviet Union]] annexed it in 1939, Lviv lost an estimated 80–90% of its prewar population, and in February 1946 it became part of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. Its historic center, with Renaissance, Baroque, and Art Nouveau architecture, is a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] listed as endangered because of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Sweet fruit of the tree *Litchi chinensis*, the sole member of its genus in the soapberry family, Sapindaceae. The fruit has a mildly tart flavor and a rose-like aroma, and it is enclosed in a pink-red, rough-textured shell. Three subspecies are recognized, the most common of which is found in South [[China|China]], Malaysia, and northern [[Vietnam|Vietnam]]. Cultivation in China has been documented since the 11th century, and China is the main producer, followed by [[India|India]], Vietnam, other countries in [[Southeast Asia|Southeast Asia]] and [[South Asia|South Asia]], Madagascar, and South Africa. Lychee seeds contain methylene cyclopropyl glycine, which has caused [[Hypoglycemia|hypoglycemia]] linked to encephalopathy outbreaks among undernourished children in India and Vietnam who consumed the fruit.

Clade of vascular plants bearing [[Spore|spores]], including the clubmosses. Lycophytes are among the oldest lineages of living vascular plants, and extinct members date to the [[Silurian|Silurian]], c. 425 million years ago. Lycophytes dominated some [[Carboniferous|Carboniferous]] landscapes, and tree-like forms such as *Lepidodendrales* grew over 40 meters (130 ft) tall and contributed to the formation of [[Coal|coal]] deposits. Extant lycophytes are relatively small. Their leaves are microphylls with a single vein, whereas most other vascular plants, including [[Fern|ferns]], [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperms]], and [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], have more complex megaphylls. Names such as Lycophyta are used inconsistently, sometimes including the extinct zosterophylls.

Legendary lawgiver of [[Sparta|Sparta]], credited with political, economic, and social reforms that produced a military-oriented society. Almost nothing is known for certain about him, and ancient sources placed him at various times; some modern scholars deny he existed. The reforms attributed to him include the Spartan mess halls called *syssitia*, the redistribution of land to citizens, and Spartan austerity and frugality. Most of the reforms likely date to the late sixth century BC, long after his supposed life, and the land redistribution is considered fictitious. The Spartans honored him as a god, and his image was reinterpreted over time to justify later changes. Ancient sources disagreed on when he lived, as [[Plutarch|Plutarch]] noted.

Iron Age kingdom in western [[Anatolia|Anatolia]], with Sardis as its capital and only city, prominent in the 8th to 6th centuries BC. Lydia was known for its wealth in gold and for the world's first coinage; Lydian [[Coin|coins]] made of electrum date to around the 7th century BC and are among the oldest in existence. At its greatest extent in the 7th century BC, it covered all of western Anatolia. In 546 BC it became a satrapy of the [[Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid Empire]], and in 133 BC it became part of the Roman province of Asia. The Lydian language was an [[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]] language related to Luwian and Hittite, written in an alphabet related to Greek. Sardis's terracing method influenced the planning of other multi-level cities.

Common name for alkaline solutions such as [[Sodium hydroxide|soda lye]] and [[Potassium hydroxide|potash lye]]. Traditionally made by leaching wood ashes in water, lye is used to cure foods such as olives, cocoa, [[Mandarin orange|canned mandarin oranges]], pretzels, and bagels, and it is the curing agent of the Nordic lutefisk. Lye is also used in [[Ramen|ramen]] noodles and as an ingredient in [[Soap|soapmaking]]. Food-grade lye in the [[United States|United States]] must meet Food Chemicals Codex requirements, while lower grades are sold as drain and oven cleaners.

Tick-borne infection caused by *Borrelia* bacteria and the most common disease spread by [[Tick|ticks]] in the [[Northern Hemisphere|Northern Hemisphere]]. The most common sign is an expanding red rash, *erythema migrans*, which usually appears one or two weeks after a bite and is typically neither itchy nor painful. Roughly 70–80% of infected people develop it, often with fever, headache, and fatigue. If untreated, infection may cause facial palsy, joint pain and swelling, severe headaches, and heart palpitations. Treatment with [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]], such as [[Doxycycline|doxycycline]], [[Amoxicillin|amoxicillin]], or cefuroxime, usually lasts two or three weeks, and most treated patients recover fully. Prevention includes covering the arms and legs and using repellents. No human [[Vaccine|vaccine]] is currently available; LYMERix was discontinued in 2002 for lack of demand, and several vaccines protect dogs.

Network of vessels, nodes, and lymphoid organs, complementary to the [[Circulatory system|circulatory system]] and a vital part of the [[Immune system|immune system]]. Lymph originates as interstitial fluid that leaks from blood into tissues, carrying nutrients to cells and collecting waste, [[Bacteria|bacteria]], and damaged cells before draining into lymphatic vessels. The circulatory system processes about 20 liters of blood daily, and about 3 liters of fluid remain in the tissues, which the lymphatic system returns to the blood. Lymph vessels pass through lymph nodes, which filter out unwanted material and hold the highest concentration of lymphocytes, along with the [[Spleen|spleen]], thymus, and tonsils. Lymph moves by muscle contractions, and its ducts empty into the subclavian veins. The system was first described in the 17th century by Olaus Rudbeck and Thomas Bartholin.

Group of blood and lymph tumors that develop from lymphocytes, a type of [[White blood cell|white blood cell]]. The two main categories are non-Hodgkin lymphoma, about 90% of cases, and [[Hodgkin lymphoma|Hodgkin lymphoma]], about 10%. Symptoms include painless swollen lymph nodes, fever, drenching night sweats, and unintended [[Weight loss|weight loss]]. Hodgkin lymphoma is linked to [[Epstein–Barr virus|Epstein–Barr virus]] infection, while non-Hodgkin types are associated with [[HIV/AIDS|HIV/AIDS]], [[Autoimmune disease|autoimmune diseases]], and some pesticides. Diagnosis usually involves a lymph node biopsy, and treatment may include [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]] and [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]]. The five-year survival rate in the United States is 89% for Hodgkin lymphoma and 74% for non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Lymphomas caused 305,000 deaths worldwide in 2012.
